title: Colours and clothes
description: Name the colours, and say what you are wearing.
grammar: the verb llevar, and colours that change
grammarNote: A colour changes to agree with the noun: el Wearing rojo, but la camisa roja.

explanation.summary: Colours are adjectives, and they agree with the thing they describe. The rule is the opposite of English: a colour ending in -o changes to -a for a feminine noun, and a colour that ends in -e or a consonant stays the same.

sections.heading: The two endings
sections.body: Rojo becomes roja, blanco becomes blanca, but verde stays verde and azul stays azul. So you learn a colour with its ending: el vestido rojo, la camisa roja, el vestido verde, la camisa verde. If the noun is plural, the colour takes an -s: los zapatos rojos.

sections.heading: Saying what you are wearing
sections.body: You use the verb llevar: llevo el abrigo. Llevar also means to carry or to bring. As with the weather, the verb carries the meaning and the clothes follow it.

examples.en: I am wearing a blue jacket.
She is wearing a black hat.

sections.heading: Two words for the same colour
sections.body: Your vocabulary file lists the colour as a word. In a shop you would also hear the word for the object: el rojo, el azul. The second word means the colour on its own, without a noun before it.

items.note: It changes to roja before a feminine noun: la camisa roja.
It never changes: la camisa azul.
It never changes: el coche verde.
It changes to negra before a feminine noun.
It changes to blanca before a feminine noun.
Masculine: el pantalón. The plural is los pantalones.

drills.note: Rojo becomes roja before a feminine noun.

drills.meaning: I am wearing a blue jacket

drills.note: A plural noun takes an -s on the colour.

drills.meaning: she is wearing a white hat
drills.note: Blanco becomes blanca before a feminine noun, and sombrero is masculine.
